title: Economically manufacturable atomic-density defect-tolerant digital computer

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a programmable digital computer whose active devices are specified at the level of individual atoms, packed at demonstrably atomic-scale device pitch, and manufactured economically enough to deliver useful computing. It would execute stored programs reliably despite fabrication defects and variation in device behavior. Practical operation could be at room temperature or at a lower temperature if the complete system, including refrigeration, remained practical in wall-plug energy and cost. These are combined requirements for a hypothetical system, not achievements established by the supplied evidence.

Three different properties must be distinguished. Atomic precision describes how accurately particular atoms are positioned. Device pitch describes the spacing between functional devices, including the structures needed to operate them. Usable system density describes how much reliable computation and storage fit into the complete machine after accounting for wiring, memory, control, redundancy and cooling. Positioning one dopant to one lattice site establishes precision; it does not establish that whole transistors, or computers, can be packed one lattice site apart.

The breakthrough therefore spans materials, fabrication and computer engineering. Atomic fabrication must produce suitable devices at useful throughput, while architecture, memory and interconnect must turn those devices into a reliable programmable system. Defect tolerance is central: the machine must retain useful yield and performance when some devices fail or vary, without consuming its density and cost advantages in repair, replacement or redundancy.

significance.text: The 2024 IRDS roadmap motivates beyond-CMOS research by explaining that dimensional scaling of CMOS will eventually approach fundamental limits. If atomic-scale computing delivered substantially more usable devices and substantially lower cost per reliable function than advanced CMOS, it could renew the density and affordability gains historically associated with integrated circuits. The analogy concerns economical integration: atomic placement would matter because it improved complete computing systems, rather than simply producing smaller laboratory structures.

Conditional consequences include more computation and memory within a fixed volume or budget, potentially making previously expensive local computation affordable. However, the supplied evidence does not establish orders-of-magnitude gains per dollar or per cubic centimeter. Such gains would require measurements that include device footprint, memory, interconnect, fabrication throughput, yield, defect-management overhead and cooling. A small active element can still require large contacts and control structures, and additional devices are useful only if the system can communicate with and power them.

Higher density would not automatically reduce switching energy or permit arbitrary increases in operating speed. Wiring resistance, heat removal and quantum-sensitive device behavior could limit the usable advantage. IRDS identifies compatible memory, interconnect, reliability and architecture as system challenges, while NIST describes strong dependence of atomically defined devices on atomic configuration and quantum behavior. These considerations make the impact highly conditional; they do not demonstrate that the proposed computer is impossible.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability is the integration of atomic-scale device pitch, reliable stored-program computation, practical operating conditions and economical production. None of the supplied sources demonstrates that combination. The central scientific challenge is controlling device behavior when the position, type, number and arrangement of a few atoms can materially change electrical properties. Useful logic requires reproducible switching behavior and operating margins across integrated devices, rather than successful operation of one carefully prepared element.

Manufacturing must escape a throughput and expertise bottleneck. NIST describes an STM fabrication workflow that requires an expert operator and substantial human time to create a single device, restricting both complexity and mass manufacture. Its automation work addresses that problem, but automating a serial process alone does not establish an affordable factory. The proposed breakthrough needs a scalable route, such as parallel fabrication or another process whose economics are not dominated by serial probe-writing, together with reliable inspection and process control.

System integration must preserve the benefit of small devices. Memory, contacts, wiring and control cannot occupy so much area or dissipate so much energy that atomic-scale active elements provide little usable advantage. The architecture must also handle defects and variation. Candidate approaches could include testing, mapping around failed elements, redundant resources or error detection and correction, but no particular mechanism or tolerable defect rate is established here. The relevant engineering question is how much reliable computation remains after paying those overheads.

Thermal practicality is a separate barrier from atomic placement. Operation without a dilution refrigerator would still permit substantial cryogenic overhead. A convincing system must sustain its workload with acceptable total electrical input, cooling equipment, heat removal and reliability. Atomic density cannot by itself solve switching-energy dissipation, and stacking more active layers cannot by itself remove the resulting heat.

current_state.text: Fuechsle and colleagues reported a single-atom transistor in Nature Nanotechnology on February 19, 2012. The abstract describes a phosphorus dopant positioned within an epitaxial silicon device with accuracy of one lattice site and transistor operation at liquid-helium temperatures. This is a demonstration of deterministic atomic placement and cryogenic device operation. It does not establish atomic-pitch transistor arrays, room-temperature digital logic or an integrated universal processor. The supplied review had access to the abstract and subscription-preview material, not the experimental body and figures.

NIST's atom-scale device program page, updated October 5, 2026, describes efforts to control atomic and molecular placement for devices including qubits, simulators and sensors. It explains that atomic configuration strongly affects device behavior and that quantum effects are significant. Its manufacturing discussion identifies expert-operated STM fabrication and substantial human time per device as limits on complexity and mass production. Machine-learning-inspired fabrication automation is described as work toward robust manufacturability, not evidence of an economical atomic-density processor production line. The review retained the complete webpage text; referenced images were not inspected.

The 2024 IRDS Beyond CMOS roadmap identifies eventual CMOS scaling limits and challenges involving new devices, compatible memory and interconnect, reliability, materials control and architecture. It is a roadmap of research needs and options, not a report that an atomic-density classical computer has been built, nor an endorsement of a closed list of ten revolutionary discoveries. The supplied extraction ends partway through PDF page 25, so later sections, tables and figures were outside the reviewed material.

The supplied evidence establishes a dated single-atom device result and continuing fabrication challenges in a recently updated research program. It does not demonstrate the complete CPE-08 target, but it also does not establish that no qualifying system existed anywhere as of November 1, 2026. No bounded freshness search was supplied. The defensible conclusion is that completion is not established by this evidence; the limited coverage is not evidence that an unexamined result is false.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed functional milestone: demonstrate a universal stored-program processor at least at microcontroller level, with a 32-bit instruction set, kilobytes of memory and reliable execution of stored programs using the atomically specified devices. Publish the architecture, operating conditions, workload results and error measurements. These numerical thresholds are proposed milestones, not established standards. A finite program suite would establish demonstrated functional breadth, not prove correct execution of every possible program.
completion_criteria.label: Stored-program 32-bit atomic-device processor executes reliably with kilobytes of memory

completion_criteria.text: Proposed density demonstration: report atomic placement accuracy, functional device dimensions and device pitch separately, then measure usable system density including memory, interconnect, contacts, control and redundancy. Identify which computing elements actually use the atomic fabrication process and how much of the demonstrated processor depends on them. Compare the complete implementation with a stated advanced-CMOS baseline using matched functional requirements. The supplied evidence does not justify a universal numerical cutoff for atomic-density qualification.
completion_criteria.label: Usable system density and atomic device pitch versus matched advanced-CMOS

completion_criteria.text: Proposed operating demonstration: run without a dilution refrigerator and report temperature, sustained workload, throughput, error rate and total wall-plug energy, including refrigeration and supporting electronics. Show a credible thermal budget under sustained activity. Avoiding one type of refrigerator is an initial boundary; practical operation requires evidence that the full cooling and power burden is acceptable for a stated use case.
completion_criteria.label: Sustained thermal budget and full wall-plug energy, no dilution refrigerator

completion_criteria.text: Proposed manufacturing and reliability demonstration: measure fabrication defects, device variation, functional yield and the area, energy, latency and throughput costs of tolerating them. Repeat fabrication and operation across multiple devices and production runs, with independent reproduction where feasible. Demonstrate operation under a stated range of observed defects and variations, optionally supplemented by controlled fault injection. Such tests would establish a measured tolerance envelope, not immunity to arbitrary defects.
completion_criteria.label: Measured defect-tolerance envelope and resource costs across production runs

completion_criteria.text: Proposed economic demonstration: provide a quantitatively justified manufacturing route whose throughput is not dominated by serial probe-writing. Report production rate, yield, testing and repair costs, and cost per reliable function against a stated advanced-CMOS baseline. Separate measured pilot-production results from projected mature-process costs and disclose the assumptions behind those projections. A processor prototype plus a parallel-manufacturing proposal would be an important milestone; the economically manufacturable claim would require corresponding process and cost evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Cost per reliable function versus advanced-CMOS without serial probe-writing dominance

completion_criteria.text: A single cryogenic transistor, a conventional CMOS transistor with a smaller fin, an isolated steep-slope tunnel transistor or a multilayer stack of ordinary devices would not alone satisfy these proposed criteria. Each could contribute useful technology, but none by itself demonstrates the combined processor, density, defect-tolerance and manufacturing requirements.
completion_criteria.label: Combined requirements shown beyond any isolated device or ordinary stack

related_concepts.text: CPE-02, Room-temperature general-purpose adiabatic reversible computer, addresses switching-energy recovery and reversible computation. CPE-08 addresses atomic-scale integration, reliable use of imperfect devices and production economics. Atomic placement does not recover switching energy, and reversible operation does not place devices at atomic pitch. The capabilities could complement one another if heat limits the usable density of an atomic-scale machine.

CPE-03, General-purpose fabric that retires data-movement dominance, overlaps through memory placement, interconnect and architecture. An atomic-density processor could still spend most of its energy or time moving data, while a fabric that greatly reduces data movement could use conventional-size devices. Monolithic 3D integration could assist either concept, but more layers do not establish atomic device pitch or eliminate thermal constraints.

CPE-04, Cascadable general-purpose photonic computer with optical memory, changes the physical implementation of computation and memory toward optical processing. CPE-05, Mammalian-scale neuromorphic learning machine near biological energy, targets a learning architecture and energy regime. Either might benefit from dense fabrication, but neither supplied definition requires the atomically specified universal digital processor or manufacturing economics of CPE-08.

CPE-06, Wall-plug-superior superconducting classical computer at useful scale, shares the need to evaluate the complete system's power and cooling burden. CPE-08 permits practical cryogenic operation without requiring superconductivity. Conversely, a superconducting classical computer could meet its own target without atomic-density fabrication.

CPE-01, Application-scale fault-tolerant quantum computer, and CPE-07, Utility-scale quantum-repeater internet, concern quantum computation and quantum networking. Atomically defined devices can support quantum applications, as NIST's program illustrates, but those applications do not establish a classical stored-program processor. Quantum fault tolerance and the fabrication-defect tolerance required here address different system problems, even where control hardware or fabrication methods overlap.

The research's historical steep-slope logic and multilayer-integration proposals remain neighboring ideas. Steeper transistor switching could help reduce operating voltage without producing atomic-density devices; many active layers could improve volumetric integration while retaining ordinary transistors. Neither capability entails the complete CPE-08 breakthrough, and neither establishes the historical claims of extreme speed at negligible power or unlimited layers without thermal penalty. These distinctions preserve the separate identities of the supplied roster entries.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the worldwide completion status of the full target as of November 1, 2026; no bounded freshness search was provided.
A quantitative definition of qualifying atomic-scale device pitch and the required usable system-density advantage remains to be chosen.
No supported numerical target is available for cost advantage, acceptable defect rate, redundancy overhead, operating power or cooling burden.
A scalable production process and its measured throughput, repeatability, yield and cost remain unspecified in the supplied material.
The 2012 experimental body and figures, later portions of the IRDS report and NIST's referenced images were outside the reviewed evidence.

The recommendation to defer comparisons with CPE-02 and historical items 1 and 2 was not adopted because their identities and relevant descriptions are present in the final supplied inputs. Comparisons with the other roster entries remain limited to their supplied titles.

brief.title: Affordable computers built atom by atom
possible: You could fit more computing and memory into the same space or budget. The goal is a programmable computer built from devices defined atom by atom, packed at atomic spacing, that keeps working despite manufacturing flaws and can be produced affordably.
why: People priced out of demanding computing could afford to do more of it locally. As conventional chips approach limits on how small their components can become, economical atomic construction could extend gains in computing capacity and affordability.

sources.who: Martin Fuechsle, Michelle Y. Simmons and colleagues
sources.showed: They built a transistor, an electronic switch, around a phosphorus atom placed at a chosen position in a silicon crystal. It worked at liquid-helium temperatures, and measurements revealed distinct electron energy levels.
sources.quote: The transistor operates at liquid helium temperatures, and millikelvin electron transport measurements confirm the presence of discrete quantum levels in the energy spectrum of the phosphorus atom.
sources.cited_for: The work establishes precise atomic placement in a working electronic device.
sources.not_established: It does not establish closely packed arrays of working switches or a programmable computer.

sources.who: IEEE International Roadmap for Devices and Systems team
sources.showed: Their research roadmap describes limits to shrinking conventional chips and challenges for alternative devices, including memory, wiring, reliability and computer design.
sources.cited_for: The roadmap explains why smaller devices need compatible memory, wiring and system design to improve computing.
sources.not_established: A roadmap of research challenges does not demonstrate a working atomic-scale computer.

sources.who: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sources.showed: Researchers built an artificial molecule on silicon using an atom-positioning probe and measured its electron energy states. Their broader fabrication process still requires substantial expert time per device.
sources.quote: We were able to measure the highest occupied state and the lowest unoccupied state in detail and compare them to an analogous molecule in vacuum.
sources.cited_for: The work illustrates control of atomic structures and the difficulty of manufacturing them at scale.
sources.not_established: It does not demonstrate economical production of reliable programmable computers.

shown: Fuechsle and colleagues demonstrated a working single-atom transistor. NIST describes further atomic fabrication and measurement work. These are device-level achievements; the combined requirements for an affordable, densely packed computer remain undemonstrated.
missing: A complete processor must combine atomic device spacing with memory, wiring and controls without losing its space advantage.
Reliable computing must survive manufacturing defects and device variation without excessive spare hardware or repair costs.
Sustained operation must keep total electricity use and cooling practical.
A repeatable manufacturing process must deliver useful computers affordably without depending mainly on writing devices individually with a probe.

milestones.label: A working processor with memory
milestones.explanation: A processor would have to reliably run stored programs with 32-bit instructions, encoded as groups of binary digits, and kilobytes of memory. This would establish basic programmable computing with atomically specified devices.

milestones.label: A measured density advantage for the complete computer
milestones.explanation: Measurements would have to distinguish atomic placement from device spacing and compare complete computing capacity per volume with matched conventional chips. This would test whether tiny devices yield a usable space advantage.

milestones.label: Sustained operation with practical power and cooling
milestones.explanation: A sustained workload would have to run without a dilution refrigerator, a system for extreme cooling, while accounting for all electricity and heat removal. This would test practicality for a stated use.

milestones.label: Measured reliability despite defects across production runs
milestones.explanation: Repeated production runs would have to establish which defects and variations the computer tolerates, including costs in space, energy and speed. This would define the range over which it remains useful.

milestones.label: Competitive manufacturing cost backed by production measurements
milestones.explanation: Production measurements would have to justify cost per reliable computing function against conventional chips, without fabrication dominated by individual probe writing. This would establish an economical manufacturing route.

milestones.label: The combined requirements demonstrated together
milestones.explanation: A complete system would have to meet the processor, density, defect-tolerance and manufacturing requirements together. This would establish the capability beyond an isolated device or a stack of ordinary components.

uncertain: How close must working devices sit, and how much complete-system density improvement should qualify?
What cost advantage, defect tolerance and cooling burden would make the computer practical?
How much of the density advantage would survive wiring, memory, spare devices and heat removal?

page.title: Atomically precise digital computers
page.definition: A stored-program digital computer uses active devices whose defining atoms are individually specified and tolerates fabrication defects. Including memory, wiring, control, redundancy and cooling, it occupies less volume and costs less per completed workload than a CMOS computer matched for throughput and output accuracy; CMOS is the transistor technology used in conventional integrated circuits.

goal.need: DOE's 2019 project contrasted 10 nm ion-implantation placement resolution with a ±0.3 nm positioning target for dopants in silicon. These are fabrication quantities, not transistor pitch. IEEE's 2024 roadmap identifies signal gain, restoration, reliability and manufacture at low cost as additional requirements for a competing logic technology.

figures.caption: Silicon dopant placement in DOE's 2019 project description
figures.note: Placement resolution and positioning precision are different quantities; neither specifies spacing between complete devices.

completion.title: An atomically precise computer has lower total volume and workload cost than matched CMOS.
completion.criterion: A manufactured stored-program computer with atomically specified active devices executes a stated workload correctly despite characterized fabrication defects. Against a commercial CMOS system at matched throughput, latency and output accuracy, it occupies less total system volume and costs less per completed workload at the same production volume and service life. Include fabrication yield, testing, repair, memory, contacts, wiring, control, redundancy, electricity and cooling. Measure functional-device spacing separately from atomic-placement error. The cited results do not establish this combined test.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no external combined acceptance test was found in the programmes and roadmaps cited.
completion.basis: Searches of IEEE IRDS, NIST, DOE programmes and silicon-electronics reviews and roadmaps found no combined acceptance test, atomic device-pitch cutoff or computer-level cost threshold. This Atlas fallback combines their placement, logic and manufacturing goals. The matched CMOS comparison is an Atlas criterion; it does not define devices one lattice spacing apart.

milestones.title: A working atomic electronic device has active sites positioned within one silicon lattice spacing.
milestones.criterion: Fabricate and electrically characterize a device whose defining active sites are positioned to one silicon lattice spacing or better. This tests placement, not device pitch. Fuechsle et al. reported one phosphorus transistor on 19 February 2012, with one-site placement accuracy and transport measured at about 20 mK. In 2018, Huff et al. reported a wire and a two-input OR-gate design made from silicon dangling bonds, exposed atomic sites left by removing hydrogen. Measurements at 4.5 K covered all four gate-input combinations.
milestones.set_by: Atomic-device research convention used by Fuechsle et al. and documented in Schofield et al.'s 2025 roadmap, section 5.4; the quoted numerical placement capability concerns silicon dopants.

milestones.title: Atomic logic forms a complete Boolean gate set, restores signals and drives more than one following gate.
milestones.criterion: A fabricated gate set is logically complete: compositions can implement any Boolean function. It also isolates outputs from inputs, restores signal levels at each gate and drives more than one subsequent gate. Include the clock and control required to obtain those properties. Huff et al.'s OR-gate result establishes one function; their paper identifies NOT, AND and fan-out structures as further work.
milestones.set_by: IEEE IRDS Beyond CMOS Focus Team, Beyond CMOS (2024), section 7.1.1, Architectural Requirements for a Competitive Logic Device.
milestones.threshold_quote: Logical completeness (the device is capable of realizing any arbitrary logic function)

milestones.title: A scanning tunnelling microscope fabricates an atomic device without operator intervention.
milestones.criterion: Starting from an operator's fabrication-strategy input file, the scanning tunnelling microscope and its controller complete the programmed atomic-fabrication steps without operator intervention, including tip recovery and recognition of existing features. This is an automation target, not a throughput or cost threshold. NIST's page updated 5 October 2026 describes it as a goal.
milestones.set_by: NIST Atom-scale Devices: Engineering, Metrology and Manufacturability programme, Towards manufacturability section; the target concerns STM fabrication.
milestones.threshold_quote: perform all fabrication steps without operator intervention.

milestones.title: An atomic-device computer executes stored programs correctly despite characterized fabrication defects.
milestones.criterion: A physical computer uses its atomically defined devices to execute instructions stored in memory and produces the specified outputs on stated programs despite characterized fabrication defects. Implemented repair, avoidance or redundancy may provide tolerance. This is the prototype before cost and density qualification. Walter et al.'s 2023 preprint models 13 substrate-defect types; Ng et al.'s 2026 study synthesizes and simulates dangling-bond accelerator layouts. Neither is a hardware demonstration of this criterion.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback: searches of IEEE IRDS, NIST, DOE and semiconductor roadmaps found no published acceptance test for an integrated, defect-tolerant stored-program atomic computer.

not_found: No external acceptance test was found for the integrated defect-tolerant stored-program prototype or the complete volume-and-cost comparison.
No external device-pitch cutoff defining an atomic-density computer was found.
Searches of atomic-device processor demonstrations and manufacturing reports found no physical result establishing the combined completion test.
